questions.q: Why does creating a MySQL stored procedure in the command-line client require the DELIMITER trick?
options: MySQL servers reject any statement longer than one line without it
DELIMITER is required by the SQL standard for all CREATE PROCEDURE statements
The client uses ; to decide when to send a statement, but procedure bodies legitimately contain internal semicolons
MySQL procedures are not allowed to contain semicolons at all
questions.explain: Without changing the delimiter, the client would send the procedure body as soon as it hit the first internal semicolon, before the CREATE PROCEDURE statement is finished.

options: The character used to separate columns in query results
What the CLIENT TOOL treats as the end-of-statement marker, not anything on the MySQL server
The MySQL server's internal semicolon-parsing rules
The character set used for string literals
questions.explain: DELIMITER is purely a client-tool convention — the MySQL server has no concept of it.

questions.q: True or false: application code using a MySQL driver (Python, Java, .NET) needs to issue DELIMITER before creating a stored procedure.
options: True — every language's MySQL driver requires it
True, but only for procedures longer than 10 lines
False — drivers send the whole procedure body as one string, with no client prompt to confuse
False, but only when using InnoDB tables
questions.explain: DELIMITER exists only because interactive CLI tools need to know where a statement ends when it contains semicolons — drivers don't have that ambiguity.

questions.q: After defining a procedure with DELIMITER $$, what should you do before writing normal SQL statements again?
options: Restart the MySQL server
Nothing — the client automatically resets after one statement
Run DROP DELIMITER;
Run DELIMITER ; to restore the standard semicolon as the statement terminator
questions.explain: DELIMITER ; switches the client back to treating semicolons as the normal end-of-statement marker.

questions.q: What keyword executes a stored procedure in MySQL, once it's created?
options: INVOKE
RUN
EXEC
CALL
questions.explain: MySQL uses CALL ProcedureName(); T-SQL uses EXEC — a real, simple syntax difference to remember.
